newsitem.title: USA: Shoppers find unleavened bread is anything but flat.
newsitem.headline: Shoppers find unleavened bread is anything but flat.

text.p: Matzo, the traditional Passover staple, may indeed be unleavened bread, but you sure need a lot of dough to buy it.
In fact, matzo prices are so high that shoppers in Florida, which has a large Jewish population, complained to Representative Robert Wexler, a Florida Democrat.
Wexler, in turn, asked Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth to launch an investigation into whether distributors and manufacturers have broken any price-fixing laws.
"We're investigating to determine if there is any illegal price-fixing or collusion," said Bob Buchner, an assistant attorney general in Butterworth's office.
"The investigation stems from the fact that it appears that the price for matzo is signficantly higher here than it is in other places," Buchner said.
"We've heard prices of $12.99 for a five pound box of matzo in Florida, compared with $4.95 a box in New York," he said.
Butterworth last week issued subpoenas to two matzo manufacturers, B. Manishewitz Co. and Aron Streit Inc., and seven distributors.
"It's not illegal to set prices anyway you want to, but it is if companies are getting together to do that," he said.
Matzo manufacturers said they have raised the price they charge to distributors to reflect higher costs, but that they have nothing to do with selling at the retail level.
"We have one price that we charge to distributors all over the country. We don't get involved in the selling prices. " said Franklin Claire, vice president of Manishewitz, based in Jersey City, N.J.

Indeed, the price for a five-pound package of wafer-like crackers varies widely even within the same city. The price hikes are most noticeable at small speciality stores, which can not afford to offer discounts that are available at the larger chains.
"We have some major retailers who discount and sell it at a loss," said Claire.
Mel Gross, vice president of Aron Streit Inc. in New York City, said the company has raised prices it charges to distributors due to labour and raw material increases.
"We fix nothing. We fix no prices. Basically, some retailers tend to make this a very aggressive marketing tool.

"In New York, you can get five pounds of matzo for free if you buy $50 worth of groceries at certain retailers. In other cities, where there's a lack of competition, a five pound box is selling for $14.99," he said.
Gross said that Passover accounts for 70 percent of Streit's annual business. The eight-day holiday begins the evening of Monday, April 21.

"If a small merchant buys it, he wants to make a profit so he raises his prices," said Rabbi Shalom Meir Ohana, director of products and ingredients in Kosher Overseers Association of America Inc., a company in Los Angeles that certifies kosher products.
Ohana also pointed out that matzo made specially for the first two nights of Passover involves extensive work and timing, which drives up its cost.
"It could vary between $10 and $17 a box, but I'm hearing that people are getting it for $12 to $12.50 a box," he said, referring to the special matzo.
Buchner said the subpoenaed companies have until May 13 to respond.
"If we determine that there is collusion, there could be substantial civil penalties," he said.
